migration is cheaper than the coordination cost of not doing it. Decided by the owner
2026-07-26 on the reasoning in nocx-6zu5.

## The surface, measured 2026-07-26

MIGRATES to Solid — 4,731 lines of ordinary application UI:

| file | lines | | file | lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| connections.ts | 872 | | export-section.ts | 519 |
| settings.ts | 786 | | profiles.ts | 348 |
| tab-strip.ts | 596 | | settings-content.ts | 334 |
| tabs.ts | 585 | | main.ts | 288 |
| sidebar.ts | 164 | | banner.ts | 139 |
| agent-status.ts | 43 | | connections-content.ts | 49 |
| native-mode.ts | 8 | | | |

STAYS imperative or framework-neutral — 4,344 lines:
terminal-content.ts 570, renderers/ 690, scrollback/ 1296, editor.ts 196, input-state.ts
100, input-target.ts 64, dispatcher.ts 254, gutter.ts 204, command-ledger.ts 203,
clipboard.ts 210, frame.ts 68, submit.ts 15, ipc.ts 474.

Note the split is not "old vs new". `ipc.ts` and `dispatcher.ts` are PROTOCOL and stay
plain TypeScript permanently — framework-neutral, not "not yet migrated". The terminal
files stay imperative permanently by AD-6.

`tabs.ts` (585) is the boundary file and the hardest single item: TabManager is part tab
list (migrates) and part terminal lifecycle (must not). Split it before migrating it.

## Non-negotiable boundary — AD-6

Solid creates an EMPTY host element. The terminal adapter takes exclusive ownership of its
descendants. Solid may control the host's placement, size, classes and visibility, and
must never:
- render children beneath it,
- key or remount it during ordinary tab activation — that risks session loss, WebGL churn
  and Linux repaint regressions,
- express terminal render state, buffers, selections or per-cell data as reactive state.

Disposal is owned exactly once. ADR-0005's WebKitGTK refresh pump stays wholly inside the
terminal controller; Solid effects must never drive terminal refreshes, and the framework
does not "solve" that pump — it addresses compositor presentation, not DOM diffing.

## Migration method — strangler, and migrated surfaces are REWRITTEN

Wrapping the existing DOM-building classes in Solid components without changing their
ownership preserves the exact defects this exists to remove. nocx-x6w9 (settings chrome
built twice by two modules) is the proof: it is an ownership failure, not a rendering one.

Order:
1. Solid mounts one application root for the shell. Lint gate lands with it (below).
2. Application state module: Solid signals/stores hold ACCEPTED state only.
3. Framework-neutral clients and transition functions stay in plain .ts — wire parsing,
   revision validation, session transitions, command construction. Authority is encoded in
   the type: no transition may produce a server session id except by handling the
   backend's successful open response (AD-7); a settings snapshot carries its revision and
   an incoming one must pass the revision policy before replacing the local mirror.
4. Split tabs.ts along the boundary; terminal host adapter with mount/dispose counters.
5. Component primitives: button, checkbox, select, text field, search field, toolbar,
   section, dialog.
6. Migrate surface by surface: shell and tab strip, sidebar, settings, connections and
   profiles, export section, banner.
7. Delete each imperative implementation as its replacement lands. A surface is not
   migrated while both versions exist.

## Lint gate, landing in step 1 and not later

Pin `eslint-plugin-solid` (0.14.5 declares eslint ^9 and ships flat-config ESM exports —
verified compatible with this repo's eslint.config.mjs). Enable at minimum no-destructure,
reactivity, no-react-deps, no-react-specific-props, prefer-for, prefer-show,
components-return-once.

Then the part that is easy to skip and must not be: a NEGATIVE FIXTURE file containing
every prohibited pattern, with CI asserting lint FAILS on it. The plugin was last
published 2024-12-11, about nineteen months ago. Without a self-testing fixture, a future
ESLint or TypeScript upgrade can silently disable a rule and the mitigation evaporates
without anyone noticing. That fixture is what makes this decision safe; it is a
deliverable of this epic, not a nice-to-have.

## Explicitly out

- Solid 2.x. Pin 1.x, write against Solid 1 semantics, build no 2.x compatibility
  abstractions, revisit only when 2.0 is stable and offers nocx something concrete.
- Zustand or any second state library (see nocx-ycet).
- A prebuilt visual component suite — it will fight the terminal aesthetic and carry
  styling assumptions unsuited to embedded webviews. Small local kit only.
- Rewriting the terminal, renderers, scrollback, editor internals or the protocol layer.
- SSR, routing, and any web-target concern. This is a webview app.
- New features. Every migrated surface keeps its current behaviour; behaviour changes are
  their own beads. A rewrite that also redesigns cannot be reviewed.

## Verification

The webview is WKWebView / WebView2 / WebKitGTK, not Chromium. "Works in Chrome" is not
evidence. Each migrated surface keeps its vitest coverage, and the e2e suite must stay
green on the headless devharness path throughout — including the terminal mount/dispose
counters, which are what prove the AD-6 boundary held.

## Success Criteria

No module under frontend/src builds application UI imperatively except the terminal
boundary files listed above; a single Solid root owns the shell; application state lives
in one Solid store with authority and transition rules in framework-neutral TypeScript;
every control comes from the local component kit; `eslint-plugin-solid` runs in the gate
with a negative fixture that CI proves still fails; the terminal mounts and disposes
exactly once across tab switches and closes, asserted by test; the full local gate and the
e2e suite are green; and every imperative predecessor file is deleted rather than left
beside its replacement.
notes:
SEQUENCING NOTES 2026-07-26.

BLOCKS FIVE EPICS, and the freeze is the honest consequence of a rewrite rather than an oversight. Each edge is a real file collision, not a schedule:
- nocx-ycet (frontend state) — main.ts, tabs.ts, tab-strip.ts, sidebar.ts. Also largely ABSORBED: Solid brings its own reactive state, so what survives is the slice-ownership map and the authority boundary, not a library choice.
- nocx-vxqj (UI kit) — settings.ts, settings-content.ts, connections.ts, sidebar.ts, style.css. Re-scoped in shape: the kit becomes Solid components.
- nocx-708q (multi-view sidebar, file tree) — sidebar.ts, and the tree should be built natively in Solid with @tanstack/virtual-core rather than hand-rolled then rewritten.
- nocx-9le (SSH client) — connections.ts (872) and profiles.ts (348) both migrate.
- nocx-8yg (Terminal UI: fonts, themes, hotkeys) — the settings surface and styling.

DELIBERATELY NOT BLOCKED: nocx-2gf (CodeMirror 6) and nocx-4ff (command input and blocks). Both live in the files that stay imperative — editor.ts, input-state.ts, input-target.ts, dispatcher.ts, gutter.ts, command-ledger.ts. They can run in parallel with this epic provided the AD-6 boundary holds, and freezing them would stop the two tracks vision.md puts first for no file-level reason.

ONE ORDERING REQUEST that is not expressible as an epic edge: the open P0 input bugs nocx-4ff.28 (new tab kills input in the first tab) and nocx-4ff.29 (tab switch drops keystrokes until a click) touch tabs.ts, which this epic rewrites. Land them FIRST. Fixing a bug in code about to be rewritten is still worth it — the fix becomes behaviour the migration must preserve, and a test that pins it. Migrating first means carrying a known-broken behaviour across a rewrite and losing the ability to tell a migration regression from the original defect.

Same argument, lower stakes, for nocx-x6w9 (settings chrome rendered twice): it is the canonical example of the ownership failure this epic exists to remove, so it is worth fixing first purely so the migration has a correct target to reproduce.
CORRECTION 2026-07-26. The sequencing note above claimed nocx-4ff.28 and nocx-4ff.29 'touch tabs.ts, which this epic rewrites'. That was asserted without checking and it is WRONG.

Located by reading the code: both bugs live in frontend/src/terminal-content.ts, not tabs.ts.
- terminal-content.ts:261 — a 'focus bounce' handler bound to focusin. It only fires when something inside already receives focus, so activating a tab where nothing takes focus never triggers it. That matches nocx-4ff.29 exactly: typing does nothing until a click, because the click is what produces focusin.
- terminal-content.ts:276 — _globalKeydown, a GLOBAL listener guarded only by 'if (!target.isConnected) return'. Every tab registers one. An inactive tab's target can still be connected (in the DOM, hidden), so multiple tabs' handlers run for the same keystroke. That is the leading candidate for nocx-4ff.28.

terminal-content.ts (570 lines) and editor.ts (196) are in this epic's STAYS-IMPERATIVE set — they are terminal-adjacent and AD-6 keeps them out of Solid. So the migration does not touch this code and WILL NOT FIX THESE BUGS. They must be fixed on their own merits, and the ordering argument in the previous note ('the fix becomes behaviour the migration must preserve') does not apply, because there is no migration of that file to preserve it through.

The bugs and the migration are therefore INDEPENDENT, not sequential. They can run in parallel — different files, no collision.

FOUND IN PASSING, worth its own bead: createRegistry() in input-target.ts has no production caller. TerminalContent instantiates ShellInputTarget directly (terminal-content.ts:178) and calls submit() on it (line 199). The InputTargetRegistry abstraction from ADR-0004 section 3 is unused frontend dead code. Our deadcode gate (nocx-ckoy.1) is Go-only, which is why nothing flagged it.
BEHAVIOUR NOT TO PRESERVE — added 2026-07-26 because the scope section as written is dangerous on its own.

The epic says 'Every migrated surface keeps its current behaviour.' Taken literally by a worker, that instruction REPRODUCES the known defects, because a worker migrating settings.ts sees the duplicated chrome and faithfully rebuilds it as 'current behaviour'. These are the exceptions, and they are acceptance criteria of the migration rather than separate fixes:

- nocx-x6w9 — settings.ts and settings-content.ts each build a search box and a modified-filter. The migrated Settings surface has EXACTLY ONE of each. This is the canonical example of the ownership failure the whole epic exists to remove; fixing it separately first would be throwaway work.
- nocx-ucxl — clicking a section in the settings rail changes nothing in the content pane. The migrated surface makes section selection produce a visible change every time.
- nocx-rp2j — a cold start opens an empty panel because view registration mixes panel-views and tab-action entries in one list. The migrated sidebar has no empty-panel state at cold start, and panel-views and tab-actions are separate concepts.

METHOD, and this is the part that is easy to get wrong: for each of the three, write the BEHAVIOURAL test NOW, before the migration, marked skipped with a reference to this epic. The test survives the rewrite; the fix would not. Un-skip it as its surface is migrated. That is what makes the difference between 'the migration regressed this' and 'this was always broken' checkable after the fact, and it costs a test rather than a fix plus a rewrite of the fix.

NOT in this list, because the migration does not touch their files and they must be fixed on their own merits: nocx-4ff.28 and nocx-4ff.29 (terminal-content.ts, kept imperative by AD-6) and nocx-mqie.1 (window geometry, Go/Wails side in main.go).
TEST POLICY, decided 2026-07-26 by the owner. This SUPERSEDES two earlier statements in this epic: the success criterion 'each migrated surface keeps its vitest coverage', and the method in the BEHAVIOUR-NOT-TO-PRESERVE note that says to write behavioural tests now and mark them skipped.

The starting proposal was to delete all tests and port only production code. Measured, that is 9,135 lines of unit test plus an 802-line e2e suite, and the measurement is what changed the answer. Tests were re-sorted by WHAT THEY ASSERT rather than by which file they sit next to:

KEEP, untouched:
- e2e (12 specs, 802 lines). It asserts behaviour, not structure, so it is the only thing that survives a rewrite by construction and the only way to tell a migration regression from a pre-existing defect. playwright.config.ts already runs chromium AND webkit deliberately — nocx-q18's glyph corruption reproduces in WKWebView and not Chromium.
- ~3,928 lines on files that do not migrate (ipc.test.ts 987, scrollback/ 876, dispatcher 356, command-ledger 338, clipboard 300, editor, gutter, frame, input-state). Deleting these buys zero migration speed because the code under them never moves.
- tabs.test.ts (1,377) and test-support/tabs-fixtures.ts (341). This was the correction that mattered: they were first classified as disposable because tabs.ts migrates. Counted 2026-07-26 — 53 tests, 'mount' appearing 66 times, viewport 11, dispose 7, singleton 4, MRU 3, abort 1. That is a test of the AD-6 lifecycle contract, not of markup. 'Attached to a migrating file' does not mean 'migration-disposable'.
- profiles.test.ts and agent-status.test.ts (~141) — a client and a pure function, both framework-neutral.

DELETE, but per file and only in the commit that lands its replacement: settings.test.ts, tab-strip.test.ts, settings-content.test.ts, connections, sidebar, banner, export-section — about 2,900 lines of DOM-structure assertions. Mechanically porting these re-encodes the old design into the new code, which is the exact failure the epic's 'rewrite, do not wrap' rule exists to prevent.

METHOD PER SURFACE, replacing the skipped-spec approach: write a characterization test for observable behaviour, MAKE IT GREEN AGAINST THE OLD IMPLEMENTATION, rewrite the surface, keep it green, then delete the structural test and the predecessor file together. A skipped test proves nothing — it never ran against the old code, so it is a wish rather than a contract, and it rots with its fixtures. Running it against the old implementation first is what turns it into evidence. Cost is roughly a day across all surfaces and it is the difference between 'the migration regressed this' and 'this was always broken' being answerable.

Net: about 2,900 lines deleted rather than 9,937 — the wholesale proposal was roughly three times larger than what the evidence supports, and most of the excess was tests on code this epic never touches.

Second opinion from codex on 2026-07-26 argued the tabs.test.ts reclassification and the characterization-over-skip method independently; both were then verified against the source before being adopted.
close_reason:
EPIC COMPLETE — the application UI runs on SolidJS. 14/14 children closed.

Against the epic's own success criterion, verified on the tree: no module under frontend/src builds application UI imperatively except the boundary files AD-6 keeps that way; a single Solid root (App.tsx) owns the shell and renders empty hosts; application state lives in one Solid store with authority and transition rules in framework-neutral TypeScript (settings-domain.ts, state/); every control comes from the local kit (frontend/src/ui/, 7 components — dialog deliberately not built because no surface uses a modal); eslint-plugin-solid runs in the gate at error on .ts as well as .tsx with a negative fixture that CI proves still fails; the terminal mounts and disposes exactly once across tab switches and closes, asserted by tabs.test.ts which passed UNCHANGED through the shell migration; the full local gate and the e2e suite are green; and every imperative predecessor is deleted rather than left beside its replacement.

Surfaces migrated in order: banner (pilot), sidebar, export-section, connections, settings, tab strip, then the App root. Three defects were fixed inside the migrations that caused them rather than as separate patches — nocx-x6w9, nocx-ucxl, nocx-rp2j — all pinned by tests.

Bundle: 623,145 raw / 162,827 gzip, about +7 KB gzip net against the pre-adoption baseline and a 25-35 KB budget.

FIVE EPICS UNBLOCKED by this landing: nocx-ycet (largely absorbed — the store shipped here), nocx-vxqj (the kit shipped here, so what remains is scope), nocx-708q, nocx-9le, nocx-8yg. Whoever picks those up should re-read them against what actually shipped rather than against their original text.

WHAT THE EPIC COST IN MISTAKES, worth reading before the next one: the only real regression was an AD-6 ordering bug that 544 unit tests and every Chromium spec missed and WebKit caught; three workers reported green gates with everything uncommitted, and one accepted revision was lost because the coordinator reviewed a worktree instead of a commit before deleting it. Both lessons are in the memories.

title: ADR: decide the frontend UI layer — vanilla TS was never chosen, it was scaffolded
description:
There is no recorded decision to build the frontend in vanilla TypeScript. Asked directly
on 2026-07-26 whether it was deliberate, the honest answer from the repo is no.

Evidence:
- `frontend/` was created whole in the first commit, `2bb8ddf` "M0 scaffold: Go module +
  Wails v2 app + ghostty-web frontend skeleton", described only as "TypeScript + Vite".
  It closed nocx-29e.1 / nocx-29e.3, neither of which posed a framework question.
- `docs/architecture.md` describes the frontend as "an xterm.js (WebGL) frontend" and
  names no UI layer at all. The module map lists `terminal`, not a rendering approach for
  everything around it.
- ADR-0001 decided xterm.js as the VT engine. That is the terminal grid, not the app UI.
- No ADR in docs/decisions/ mentions React, Svelte, Vue, Solid, or a framework choice.
- `frontend/package.json` devDependencies are eslint, prettier, typescript, vite, vitest.
  No framework has ever been added or removed.

So the default arrived with the scaffold and was never revisited. That was fine while the
frontend was a terminal grid and little else. It stopped being fine this week.

## Why this is now urgent rather than academic

Three epics filed on 2026-07-26 are all downstream of this answer, and all three were
scoped assuming the default holds:

- nocx-ycet (authoritative frontend state) — its description says "EXPLICITLY OUT:
  adopting a UI framework ... this epic must not smuggle one in." That constraint was
  written believing a decision existed to respect. It did not.
- nocx-vxqj (UI kit) — its ADR asks hand-rolled components versus a headless library, and
  notes most headless libraries assume a framework. That question is unanswerable while
  this one is open.
- nocx-708q (multi-view sidebar with a file tree) — the reference implementation in Orca
  is React and ~6,900 lines for the explorer alone.

Deciding those three separately, each nudging the answer, is how a framework arrives by
accident rather than by choice — the same way vanilla did.

## The real argument, both directions

FOR staying vanilla:
- AD-6 gives terminal render state to the frontend and xterm.js owns its own DOM and WebGL
  surface. A VDOM must never diff over that; any framework adoption has to carve the
  terminal out explicitly, and that seam is a permanent cost.
- Startup time and bundle size matter more in a desktop shell than on the web.
- Fewer dependencies is a smaller supply-chain surface, which matters disproportionately
  for a tool whose pitch includes a secrets vault.
- The Go side is already interface-first with DI; the discipline exists without a
  framework enforcing it.

AGAINST:
- Everything that is NOT the terminal grid is ordinary application UI — settings,
  connections, sidebar, file tree — and that is precisely where the defects are landing.
  nocx-x6w9 (settings renders its chrome twice), nocx-ucxl (section nav does nothing),
  nocx-rp2j (empty panel at cold start) are all state-and-rendering bugs in hand-rolled
  imperative DOM code.
- The file tree in nocx-708q needs virtualised rows, lazy expansion and fs-watcher
  reconciliation. That is the kind of thing a framework ecosystem hands you.
- nocx-ycet exists because state is reduced in several places that must agree by hand.
  That is the failure mode frameworks were built to remove.

## What this bead must produce

An ADR in docs/decisions/, and it must answer at least:
1. Vanilla, or a framework, or a middle path (a small reactive/signals library with no
   VDOM, keeping direct DOM control). Name what was rejected and why.
2. If a framework: how the xterm.js surface is carved out so nothing diffs over it, and
   what happens to the ~2,500 lines of existing imperative UI — rewritten, wrapped, or
   left alone at a boundary.
3. If vanilla: what replaces the ergonomics we are giving up, concretely enough to be
   checkable — that answer is what nocx-ycet and nocx-vxqj then implement.
4. Either way: the cost of the migration measured against the three epics above, not in
   the abstract.

## Acceptance Criteria

An ADR is merged in docs/decisions/ that records the frontend UI-layer decision, the
alternatives weighed, the xterm.js boundary, and the consequences for nocx-ycet,
nocx-vxqj and nocx-708q; docs/architecture.md states the decision so it cannot be arrived
at by default a second time; and the three dependent epics have their descriptions
reconciled with whatever was decided.

## Coordinator's recommendation, 2026-07-26 (input to the ADR, not a substitute for it)

Measured: frontend/src is 9,307 non-test lines. Terminal-adjacent (terminal-content,
renderers, scrollback, editor, input-state, input-target, dispatcher, frame) is ~3,240.
Ordinary application UI (settings, settings-content, connections, profiles, sidebar,
tab-strip, tabs, export-section, banner) is ~4,390. Roughly half this frontend is not a
terminal, and nocx-708q would add thousands more.

Recommendation: **do not adopt a full framework now, and do not close this question by
default a second time.** Reasoning:

- Every UI bug filed on 2026-07-26 is a state-ownership or component-reuse failure, not a
  rendering-model failure. nocx-x6w9 is the same chrome built twice because there was
  nothing to reuse. nocx-ucxl and nocx-98z6 are state reduced in two places that must
  agree by hand. A framework would have prevented them, but so does a store plus a kit —
  which is exactly nocx-ycet and nocx-vxqj, already filed.
- A framework is a poor fit for the ~3,240 terminal lines. xterm.js owns its DOM and WebGL
  surface and AD-6 puts render state there; a VDOM must never diff over it. Adoption means
  a permanent carve-out, and that seam is a standing cost, not a one-off.
- The strongest case for adoption is nocx-708q's file tree — virtualised rows, lazy
  expansion, fs-watcher reconciliation. That is where imperative DOM genuinely hurts.

So the ADR should seriously evaluate a THIRD option that this bead's framing above
under-weights: reactive primitives / signals with no VDOM, a few KB, which supply the
state ergonomics while leaving rendering under direct control and leaving xterm alone.
That may be the actual answer, and it is the one nobody has costed.

Sequence proposed: decide here, then nocx-ycet, then nocx-vxqj, and re-open the
full-framework question explicitly at nocx-708q with measurement rather than argument.
notes:
VERIFIED 2026-07-26, and it removes an objection rather than adding one.

The owner's concern was Electron. Facts:
- Orca (the sidebar reference in nocx-708q) IS Electron: electron ^43.1.0, electron-vite ^5.0.0, React 19, and @tanstack/react-virtual for the virtualised file tree.
- Tabby is Electron too.
- nocx is NOT: Wails v2 (github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2 v2.13.0), Go plus the OS webview — WKWebView on macOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux.

CHOOSING A JS FRAMEWORK DOES NOT BRING ELECTRON. The two are independent decisions and the Electron one is already settled by the Wails shell. Wails embeds static assets; Svelte, Solid, Preact or React all compile to static JS that Wails serves identically. So 'no Electron' is not an argument for staying vanilla, and this ADR must not treat it as one.

What DOES constrain the choice, and belongs in the ADR:
- The runtime is three different OS webviews, not Chromium. ADR-0005 already documents a WebKitGTK forced-refresh pump, so the Linux webview has known rendering quirks. Framework choice must not worsen them, and 'works in Chrome' is not evidence.
- Current production bundle is 614 KB of JS with only @xterm/* as a dependency. That is the baseline any framework's cost is measured against.

Codex consulted 2026-07-26 for an outside opinion on: the signals-without-VDOM middle path, which framework suits a webview-hosted app where ~47% of the code is app UI and the rest must not be re-rendered, whether a ~4,390-line incremental migration is realistic, and whether the virtualised file tree is where vanilla stops paying.
CODEX CONSULTED 2026-07-26. It rejected the coordinator's leaning as too conservative and recommended adopting SolidJS now. Having checked its load-bearing claim, I largely agree, and the reason I was wrong is worth recording.

THE ARGUMENT THAT CHANGED MY MIND: signals fix state PROPAGATION; they do not fix component OWNERSHIP. Our worst-shaped bug, nocx-x6w9 — the settings screen rendering its search box and modified-filter twice because settings.ts and settings-content.ts independently built the same chrome — would NOT have been prevented by a signals library. It is prevented by having components. I generalised from the state bugs (nocx-98z6, nocx-ucxl) and missed that the duplication bug has a different cause.

SECOND SHARP POINT: adopting signals as a deliberate stepping stone toward a framework we believe is coming produces TWO migrations and TWO state APIs. My proposed 'revisit at nocx-708q' sequence has exactly that flaw.

CLAIM VERIFIED, since the recommendation leans on it: the production bundle is 600 KB raw / 152 KB gzip, and @xterm/xterm alone is 2.7 MB of package sources. Solid's runtime at roughly 7 KB gzip is about 5% on top of the current gzip figure. Framework weight is genuinely not an argument here.

WHAT CODEX DID NOT WEIGH, and it matters for nocx specifically: this codebase is built almost entirely by AI agents, and the agent is the labour force. Solid has a far smaller training corpus than React or Svelte, so workers will produce more idiomatic and less buggy code in a more common framework. Codex weighed ecosystem maturity for LIBRARIES but not fluency for the agents doing the work. Svelte 5 is its own stated runner-up ('I would accept it if the team strongly prefers Svelte syntax') and keeps the small runtime and the absence of a VDOM.

So the ADR's remaining question is narrower than when this bead was filed: NOT whether to adopt a framework — adopt one — but Solid vs Svelte 5, with agent fluency as an explicit weighted criterion alongside the xterm boundary and the WebKitGTK constraint.

WORTH TAKING VERBATIM INTO THE ADR, the xterm ownership contract:
1. The framework creates an EMPTY host element.
2. The terminal adapter gets exclusive ownership of its descendants.
3. The framework never conditionally inserts children into that element.
4. Reactive state crosses the boundary through explicit imperative methods (setVisible, resize, focus), never through markup describing terminal internals.
5. Disposal is owned exactly once.
Plus: never remount or re-key the terminal container on tab switches — that risks session loss, WebGL churn and Linux repaint regressions. And ADR-0005's refresh pump stays inside the xterm renderer; framework effects must not drive terminal refreshes. The pump addresses WebKitGTK compositor presentation, not DOM diffing, so a framework does not 'solve' it.

OTHER ADOPTED POINTS: set a bundle budget in the ADR (codex suggests 25-35 KB gzip for framework + store + primitives). Keep domain and protocol code framework-neutral — WSClient, dispatcher, input-state machine, terminal renderer, scrollback model, settings/profile clients must not import the framework. Migration is strangler-style surface by surface, but each migrated surface is REWRITTEN, not wrapped: wrapping the existing DOM-building classes preserves the ownership problem that caused the bugs. For nocx-708q use @tanstack/virtual-core, which is framework-agnostic — do NOT pick React merely to get @tanstack/react-virtual.

REJECTED OUTRIGHT by codex, recorded so they are not re-proposed: staying fully vanilla; signals as the final architecture; React (VDOM plus awkward imperative lifecycle for the central xterm island, and Strict Mode makes imperative resource ownership easy to get wrong); Vue (wrong weight-to-benefit); Lit as the application framework (web-component encapsulation does not address global state); RxJS or MobX as the primary store; a large prebuilt visual component suite; and a home-grown signals implementation.
DECISION REACHED 2026-07-26 after a second round with codex, in which it reversed from Solid to Svelte 5.

RECOMMENDATION FOR THE ADR: Svelte 5 in runes mode for application UI. No Zustand. Framework-neutral authority and transition logic in plain TypeScript. Exclusive imperative ownership of the xterm host subtree.

WHY SVELTE OVER SOLID — the argument is about failure mode under agent authorship, not capability. Both satisfy every technical constraint: fine-grained reactivity, no VDOM, xterm left outside the managed subtree, small runtime against a 152 KB gzip bundle, incremental migration. What separates them is that Solid uses JSX, and agents know JSX from React. That familiarity is a LIABILITY here: it invites React semantics to leak in ways that type-check and read as idiomatic in review — destructuring reactive props (silently breaks Solid reactivity), treating components as functions that re-run, wrapping derived state in effects, recreating resources expecting render cycles, confusing Show/For with JSX conditionals and .map(). Silently-wrong code that looks familiar is the worst possible defect class for an orchestrator reviewing generated diffs. Svelte's distinct syntax is protective precisely because it cannot be pattern-matched to React: wrong rune usage tends to fail loudly, and the compiler rejects or warns on more invalid constructions.

THE CAVEAT, and it must be mitigated mechanically rather than by review judgment: agents may know 'Svelte' and emit Svelte 3/4 patterns, because the Svelte-5-runes corpus is far smaller than the total Svelte corpus. Required mitigations, all gate-level:
- runes mode required for all new components
- pin the exact Svelte major.minor
- Svelte compiler checks and svelte-specific lint in the pre-commit gate
- reject legacy reactive declarations and writable stores in new application code
- a short project Svelte contract in the frontend agent instructions
- one canonical component, one shared-state module and one xterm action, provided as patterns agents copy

XTERM BOUNDARY IN SVELTE: a Svelte action, not scattered onMount code. An element using the terminalHost action MUST be empty in Svelte source; after mounting, xterm exclusively owns its descendants. Svelte may control the host's placement, size, classes and visibility. It must NOT key or remount the host during ordinary tab activation, render children beneath it, or express terminal render state as reactive state. The Linux refresh pump stays wholly inside the terminal controller.
FINAL DECISION 2026-07-26: SolidJS 1.x, pinned. This supersedes the Svelte 5 recommendation recorded in the previous note.

The Svelte recommendation rested on one claim: that Solid's React-flavoured mistakes 'type-check and look reassuringly familiar in review', making them silent under agent authorship. That claim was checked rather than accepted, and it does not hold. eslint-plugin-solid ships rules covering essentially the whole enumerated failure list — no-destructure (destructuring reactive props), reactivity (signals read outside tracked scopes), no-react-deps, no-react-specific-props, prefer-for (.map instead of For), prefer-show (JSX conditionals instead of Show), components-return-once (components treated as re-running). This repo enforces lint in the pre-commit gate and in CI, so those failures are not silent here.

Two counter-facts were found by checking symmetrically rather than only researching the preferred side, and both were weighed:
- eslint-plugin-solid is v0.14.5, last published 2024-12-11 (~19 months). eslint-plugin-svelte is v3.22.0, published 2026-07-20. The mitigation Solid depends on is far less actively maintained than Svelte's equivalent.
- solid-js stable is 1.9.14 (published 2026-07-26, so 1.x is alive) while the version list runs to 2.0.0-experimental.16. Svelte is 5.56.8, deep into a stable major.

Neither was judged decisive. A framework experimenting with its next major while maintaining the current one is normal; pin 1.x, write the ADR against Solid 1 semantics, do not build 2.x compatibility abstractions, and revisit only when 2.0 is stable and offers nocx something concrete. The stale plugin is the real risk, and it is convertible into a self-testing one — see the mandatory mitigation below.

COMPATIBILITY GATE, VERIFIED BEFORE DECIDING: eslint-plugin-solid 0.14.5 declares peerDependencies eslint ^6 || ^7 || ^8 || ^9 and typescript >=4.8.4, and ships ESM flat-config exports (./configs/recommended, ./configs/typescript, .mjs). It is compatible with this repo's ESLint 9 flat config (eslint.config.mjs, landed today via nocx-0fx). This was checked, not assumed.

MANDATORY MITIGATION, part of adoption and not optional polish — NEGATIVE LINT FIXTURES. Pin the plugin version, then add a fixture file containing every prohibited pattern (destructured props, React dep arrays, .map in JSX, JSX conditional in place of Show, a component with multiple returns, a signal read outside a tracked scope) and assert in CI that lint FAILS on it. That makes the mitigation self-testing: if an ESLint or TypeScript upgrade silently disables a rule, CI catches it instead of the defect reaching review. Without this, a 19-month-stale plugin is an unverified promise.

WHAT LINT STILL CANNOT CATCH, so the ADR states it and review covers it deliberately: reactivity hidden behind arbitrary helper functions; signals read conditionally or through aliases; values captured before entering async callbacks; owner/context lost across async work; effects that track correctly but implement the wrong ownership; unnecessary effects forming feedback loops; DOM resource cleanup bugs; and choosing a signal where a store, memo or plain value is semantically right. These are general reactive/lifecycle defects, not React-shaped ones — Svelte's compiler cannot prove them either.

STRONGEST REASON FOR SOLID: it adds component ownership to the signal-based architecture nocx already needs, without introducing either a VDOM or a second conceptual state model. The xterm boundary stays exceptionally explicit — Solid creates an empty host, an adapter mounts xterm, xterm exclusively owns the descendants.

HONEST NOTE ON PROCESS: the coordinator's position moved three times in one session — vanilla with signals, then Svelte 5, then Solid. Each move was driven by evidence that arrived, not by preference: the component-ownership argument killed signals-only; the JSX-leakage argument moved it to Svelte; the lint-coverage finding moved it back. The owner's stated preference for Solid is a legitimate tiebreaker between near-peers, and it is recorded as such — not as a technical argument. What would still change the answer: eslint-plugin-solid failing against the pinned toolchain in the fixture test above, or a bake-off showing materially more silent defects in agent-authored Solid.
close_reason:
ADR-0012 merged: docs/decisions/0012-solidjs-as-the-application-ui-layer.md (commit cd23b75).

Decision: SolidJS 1.x pinned for the application UI; xterm stays imperative behind an explicit ownership boundary; no Zustand or any second reactive system; framework-neutral protocol and authority-transition logic in plain TypeScript; eslint-plugin-solid in the gate with a negative fixture CI proves still fails.

The bead's acceptance also required architecture.md to state the decision so it cannot be arrived at by default a second time. Done in two places: the Module Map 'ui' row, and a UI-layer corollary under AD-6 that draws the Solid/xterm line — empty host, exclusive descendant ownership, no keying or remounting on tab activation, no terminal render state as reactive state, ADR-0005's refresh pump staying inside the terminal controller.

The three dependent epics are reconciled: nocx-njrx carries the migration, nocx-ycet is largely absorbed (Solid brings the container; what survives is the slice-ownership map and authority boundary), nocx-vxqj becomes a Solid component kit, nocx-708q builds its tree natively on @tanstack/virtual-core.

Falsification conditions are recorded in the ADR's 'Revisit when' rather than left implicit: the negative fixture failing to fail, evidence of materially more silent defects in agent-authored Solid, Solid 2.0 reaching stable with a concrete benefit, or the xterm boundary needing escape hatches instead of one adapter.

title: e2e is red on main: 11 failures in terminal input, focus, bell and clipboard
description:
MEASURED, not inferred. CI run 30214891053 (workflow_dispatch on main, commit 99452ba): backend PASS, frontend PASS, e2e FAIL — 11 failed, 23 passed, 2 skipped.

Failing set:
  [chromium] activity-bell.spec.ts:12   a bell lights the indicator from inside the alternate buffer
  [webkit]   activity-bell.spec.ts:12
  [chromium] click-focus.spec.ts:26     a click into the pane leaves the terminal taking keystrokes
  [webkit]   click-focus.spec.ts:26
  [chromium] clipboard.spec.ts:109      right-click pastes clipboard text at the cursor
  [chromium] enhanced-input.spec.ts:10  read command receives input after enhanced submit
  [chromium] enhanced-input.spec.ts:38  Ctrl-C at a prompt does not trap input
  [chromium] enhanced-input.spec.ts:71  multiple submits in succession all route raw
  [webkit]   enhanced-input.spec.ts:10 / :38 / :71

Shared symptom: after submit, `.tab-title` stays at the cwd ("Users/runner") instead of the
expected marker — the submitted text never reaches the PTY, or the title never updates.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out main at 99452ba (or later, if the failures persist).
2. Run the e2e suite the way CI does: `npx playwright test` (CI job `e2e`, macos-latest).
3. Observe 11 failures in the specs listed above; backend and frontend jobs stay green.

Reproduced in CI three independent times: run 30214891053 (workflow_dispatch, main, 11 fail),
run 30212570982 (PR #56, same commit as main, 12 fail = these 11 plus one clipboard:46
copy-on-select flake), run 30196746284 (PR #14, 57 commits behind main, 13 fail with the same
core plus command-editor:62).

## Why this is not a PR problem

PR #56 sits on exactly this commit (merge-base == 99452ba). Its diff is internal/ssh,
internal/profile, two profile-related frontend files and an ADR — it cannot touch terminal
focus, bell, clipboard or input routing. The direct workflow_dispatch run on main then
confirmed the baseline independently.

## Consequences

- nocx-rdkh ("The test suite is green and stays green") is closed against a red suite.
- nocx-xx56 wants to make this check required; doing so now freezes every merge.
- Fork PRs additionally need manual workflow approval, so no PR shows a check by default.

## Suspected shared root cause

nocx-4ff.28 (new tab leaves the first tab unable to accept input) and nocx-4ff.29 (switching
tabs drops keystrokes until the user clicks into the editor) describe the same class of
symptom and are both claimed. Whoever takes this must reconcile with that work rather than
fix the same defect twice.

## Acceptance Criteria

`npx playwright test` on main is green — the 11 failures above pass on both chromium and
webkit — with the root cause named and fixed in product code, not by weakening, skipping or
retry-wrapping the assertions. If any failure turns out to be a genuine test defect rather
than a product defect, that is argued explicitly in the bead before the test is changed.
close_reason: e2e is green on main. CI run 30218676302 at 84ba49d: e2e, backend and frontend all pass, against 11 e2e failures when this was filed. Four defects: nocx-hi2 (product), the title-not-empty gate mistaken for readiness, clipboard clicking stale coordinates, and the transport fairness test failing its own best case.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
RESOLVED DOWN TO ONE, and the remaining one is not this defect.

CI 30217202549 (branch shady2k/nocx-hi2-bracketed-paste-gate, macos-latest): 1 failed / 33 passed / 2 skipped, against 11 failed / 23 passed on main at 99452ba. The fix is nocx-hi2: send bracketed-paste wrappers only when the shell set DECSET 2004.

Remaining: [chromium] click-focus.spec.ts:26. It fails before the click, on the blur() precondition at line 41 — focus returns to the editor within 5s. Focus-bounce, already named as a separate fix in that test's own comment, and the same class as nocx-4ff.28/.29. Tracked there, not here.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
GREEN. CI run 30218418676 on branch shady2k/nocx-hi2-bracketed-paste-gate: e2e, backend and frontend all pass on macos-latest.

Four defects, not one, and only the first was the reason this bead was opened:

1. nocx-hi2 — bracketed-paste wrappers sent to a shell that never set DECSET 2004. macOS /bin/bash 3.2. Accounted for 10 of the original 11 failures. Fixed in product code (6ac331a).

2. The suite gated on 'tab title is non-empty' and called it 'shell is ready'. It is not: the title fills in when the session opens, while ownership of the prompt — the state in which typing reaches the editor — arrives later. Every affected spec started typing into an app that had not settled. This is why CI failed exactly ONE chromium test per run and a different one each time: 30217202549 click-focus, 30217654133 clipboard, 30217919912 enhanced-input. Replaced with promptReady() in the harness, which waits for the editor to actually hold focus (24ba31b).

3. clipboard copy-on-select measured a block's boundingBox and clicked those coordinates afterwards, while the block was still moving — collapsed selection, empty clipboard (d6bfaf5).

4. TestWSServer_FairnessTwoFloodingOneQuiet required a flood frame to arrive between the echo request and its reply. Nothing orders those frames, and the reply arriving first is the BEST case for the fairness property — the test punished it. The sound check (flood still streaming after the reply) was already present below it (bd81186).

The single-random-failure-per-run pattern was the tell: three different symptoms, one wrong precondition shared across specs.

Not closing until the branch merges.

title: Six functional options nobody passes — two of them are security controls
description:
Functional options that no caller ever passes. AGENTS.md is explicit — "YAGNI —
don't build speculative features" and "no dead code (delete it)".

From the sweep in nocx-ckoy.1:

- `internal/ssh/ssh.go:137` — `WithAuthMethods`
- `internal/ssh/ssh_real.go:21` — `WithKnownHostsFile`
- `internal/ssh/ssh_real.go:26` — `WithSSHConfigPath`
- `internal/transport/ws_auth.go:164` — `WithTokenSource`
- `internal/transport/ws_auth.go:171` — `WithOriginPolicy`
- `internal/transport/ws_auth.go:130` — `PinnedOriginPolicy.Allow`

Two of these deserve a second look rather than deletion on sight, because an
unused SECURITY option may mean the security control is not being applied at
all, which is a different and worse problem than dead code:

- `WithOriginPolicy` / `PinnedOriginPolicy.Allow` — if nothing installs an
  origin policy, what does the WebSocket handshake actually enforce today?
  Answer that before deleting. If the answer is "nothing", this bead spawns a
  security bug and the option gets WIRED, not removed.
- `WithKnownHostsFile` — same question for SSH host-key verification. Confirm
  the default path is applied through another route before concluding the
  option is merely unused.

The rest are ordinary speculative API and can go.

## Steps to Reproduce

```bash
deadcode ./... | grep -E "With[A-Z]|PinnedOrigin"
grep -rn "OriginPolicy\|knownHosts" --include=*.go internal/ | grep -v _test
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- The origin-policy and known-hosts questions are answered in writing before any
  deletion, and a security bug is filed if either control is unenforced.
- Options confirmed as speculative are deleted along with their tests.
- Options that turn out to be needed are wired at the composition root and have
  a test that exercises them through it.
- None of the six remain in the deadcode baseline.

title: Profile grouping and SSH-option merging exist twice — the Go copy is unreachable
description:
Profile group-tree construction and group-path resolution are implemented twice
— once in Go, once in TypeScript — and only the TypeScript copy runs.

Verified on main 2026-07-26 via the deadcode sweep in nocx-ckoy.1:

- Live: `frontend/src/profiles.ts:97 buildGroupTree()` and
  `profiles.ts:117 resolveGroupPath()`, both called from `connections.ts`
  (L167, L219).
- Unreachable: `internal/profile/profile.go:263 BuildGroupTree` and
  `profile.go:298 ResolveGroupPath`, along with `applyDefaults` (L134),
  `mergeSSHOptions` (L153), `mergeInto` (L166), `NewProfileID` (L212),
  `isNamespacedID` (L217), `parseNamespacedID` (L223), `expandFromMap` (L284),
  `currentUser` (L324) and `store.go:48 NewJSONStore` — 11 funcs in total.

Two implementations of one rule will drift, and the tests on the Go side will
keep passing while they do, because the Go side is not what the user exercises.
`applyDefaults` and `mergeSSHOptions` are the dangerous pair: profile default
and inheritance semantics silently defined in two places, with the authoritative
one being the untested-in-anger frontend copy.

This is also the shape of nocx-49x ("four SSH options are editable, persisted
and never applied") — worth checking whether that bug's root cause is exactly
`mergeSSHOptions` being unreachable. Do that check before designing a fix; if it
is the same cause, the two beads should be merged.

## Steps to Reproduce

```bash
deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/profile' ./...
grep -n "buildGroupTree\|resolveGroupPath" frontend/src/connections.ts
```

Observed: the Go grouping/merging logic has no caller reachable from `main()`;
the equivalent TypeScript runs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One implementation per rule. Decide deliberately which side owns profile
  defaults, SSH option merging, ID namespacing and group-tree construction, and
  say why — a Go-side answer keeps the rule testable and shared with any future
  non-web frontend, a TS-side answer keeps it where the UI already needs it.
- The losing side is deleted, not left in place "in case".
- Whichever side wins, `nocx-49x` is re-checked against it — either fixed by
  this change or explicitly confirmed to be a separate cause.
- `deadcode` reports no unreachable funcs in `internal/profile`.

title: golangci-lint cannot catch unwired subsystems — add deadcode reachability to the gate
description:
`unused` is enabled in .golangci.yml and it is not the linter that could have
caught the unwired vault (nocx-25k9.1). It answers "is this symbol referenced
anywhere in the module, tests included?" — and `NewVault` IS referenced, by
`credential_test.go:105`. The linter is correct and silent. No configuration of
`unused` changes that.

The question nobody was asking is "is this reachable from `main()`?" That is
reachability analysis from an entry point, and the official Go tool for it is
`golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode`.

Measured on main 2026-07-26:

```
$ golangci-lint run ./internal/credential/...     # clean, exit 0
$ deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/credential' ./...
  26 unreachable funcs — the entire vault, including deriveKey,
  encryptGCM, decryptGCM, Vault.Unlock, Vault.SaveSecret
```

Repo-wide: **73 unreachable funcs, 66 excluding frontend/node_modules.** The
vault is 26 of them. The rest is a useful map of the same failure mode:

- `internal/profile` (11) — `BuildGroupTree`, `ResolveGroupPath`,
  `applyDefaults`, `mergeSSHOptions`, `NewJSONStore`. Note that
  `frontend/src/profiles.ts` has its own live `buildGroupTree()` and
  `resolveGroupPath()`. The grouping logic was written twice and the Go copy is
  the dead one. Worth its own bead — filed separately.
- `internal/ssh` (13) and `internal/pty`, `internal/transport` — `NewStub`,
  `StubChannel` and friends: test doubles living in NON-test files, which is
  why they are analysed at all. `deadcode` ignores `_test.go` by default, so the
  fix for most of these is moving them where they belong.
- Unused functional options: `WithAuthMethods`, `WithKnownHostsFile`,
  `WithSSHConfigPath`, `WithTokenSource`, `WithOriginPolicy`. Speculative API —
  AGENTS.md says YAGNI and no dead code.
- `internal/settings` (4) — `MustRegisterString`, `MustRegisterNumber`,
  `MustRegisterSecret`. Corroborates nocx-i1h0 independently: those control
  types are unreachable because nobody has ever registered a string, number or
  secret setting.

IMPORTANT for whoever implements this: run `deadcode` WITHOUT `-test`. Adding
`-test` makes tests entry points, which makes the vault "reachable" again and
destroys exactly the signal we want. The consequence is that genuine test-only
helpers must live in `_test.go` files; `internal/credential/vault_testhelpers.go`
is a non-test file and shows up for that reason.

## Steps to Reproduce

```bash
go install golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode@latest
deadcode ./... | grep -v node_modules | wc -l    # 66
golangci-lint run ./...                          # clean
```

Observed: the gate is green while a whole encrypted-secrets subsystem is
unreachable from the binary.
Expected: shipping a subsystem no entry point reaches is caught before merge.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `deadcode` runs in the pre-commit hook and in CI, over the same package set as
  `golangci-lint`, excluding `frontend/node_modules`.
- The findings that exist today are resolved rather than baselined wholesale:
  each is deleted, wired, or moved into a `_test.go` file. Anything deliberately
  kept has an inline justification and appears in an explicit, reviewed
  allowlist — not a blanket suppression.
- The allowlist is small enough to read, and adding to it is a visible diff.
- README/AGENTS.md document what the check answers and why `unused` does not
  answer it, so the next person does not re-litigate this.
acceptance_criteria: deadcode runs in the pre-commit hook and in CI over the same package set as golangci-lint, excluding frontend/node_modules; a checked-in baseline file records the 66 findings that exist today and the check fails on any finding NOT in it; the check ALSO fails when the baseline grows — a ratchet, so the only permitted direction is smaller; every baseline entry names the bead that will remove it, and an entry with no bead is itself a failure; README/AGENTS.md document what the check answers and why 'unused' cannot answer it.
notes:
DECISION 2026-07-26 (owner): baseline now, block new. Do NOT wait for the cleanup — the gate lands first with the 66 current findings frozen, so that from that day on any newly-orphaned function fails the commit.

The owner named the risk with this option: an allowlist people top up instead of draining. Two mechanisms are therefore part of the acceptance criteria, not optional polish:

1. A RATCHET. The check fails if the baseline file gains entries, not only if an unlisted finding appears. Adding to the baseline must require deliberately editing the ratchet, which is a visible and arguable diff — not a passive side effect of committing dead code.
2. EVERY baseline entry names its removal bead. An entry with no bead fails the check. This is what stops the file becoming a graveyard: each line is a promise somebody can be held to, and the beads already exist for most of them (see below).

Ownership of the 66, so no line is unaccounted for:
- internal/credential (26) — nocx-25k9.1. FROZEN until that ADR decides keychain vs vault; deleting the vault before the decision would pre-empt it.
- internal/profile (11) — nocx-hhj3 (logic duplicated in TS, Go copy dead).
- internal/settings (4) — MustRegisterString/Number/Secret become reachable the moment somebody registers a setting of that type; nocx-i1h0 does the inventory. Expected to resolve by being USED, not deleted.
- stubs in ssh/pty/transport and the speculative With* options — the two cleanup beads filed alongside this one.

title: The vault is unreachable: the app wires the OS keychain and never constructs a Vault
description:
The vault is built, hardened and tested, and no shipped code path reaches it.
Secrets go to the OS keychain instead. Nobody chose that — it is what the
composition root happens to wire.

Verified on main 2026-07-26:

- `internal/app/app.go:81` wires `credential.NewKeychain()` as the
  `CredentialStore`. That instance is what reaches the settings registry (L82),
  the transport (L88) and the SSH profile resolver (L89).
- `credential.NewCredentialStore(v *Vault)` — the adapter that puts the vault
  behind the same `SecretStore` interface — is called from
  `credential_test.go:107` and nowhere else.
- `NewVault()` is called from `credential_test.go:105` and
  `vault_testhelpers.go:8`. Nowhere else in the repo.
- No vault RPC method exists in `internal/transport/ws.go`, and the frontend
  mentions the vault only in two comments (`profiles.ts:76`, `sidebar.ts:8`).

So `internal/credential/vault.go` — ~400 lines of AES-GCM, PBKDF2 key
derivation, passphrase unlock and lock/unlock state — is reachable only from
its own tests. The code's own comment says how it happened
(`credential.go:14-19`): `CredentialStore` is a type alias kept "only to avoid
editing app.go in this wave". The wave ended; app.go was never edited.

Three consequences that make this worth a bead rather than a note:

1. **A settled-looking decision was never made.** nocx-25k9 says the choice
   between an OS-keychain-backed and an app-managed store "belongs in this epic
   as an ADR before any UI work". In practice the keychain already won, by
   default, in the composition root. Either ratify that in the ADR or wire the
   vault — but stop shipping a state where the code says one thing and the
   binary does another.
2. **Three closed beads hardened unreachable code.** nocx-1vr (AES-CBC to AEAD),
   nocx-l7o (non-serializable VaultSecret) and nocx-dcd (hand-rolled PBKDF2)
   all did real security work on a path no user reaches. That is not wasted if
   the vault is going to be wired; it is pure cost if it is not.
3. **AGENTS.md forbids dead code.** 400 lines of crypto reachable only from
   tests is exactly that. Deleting it is a legitimate outcome of the decision
   below — it is NOT a legitimate thing to do before the decision.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not a runtime symptom — a wiring fact. To see it:

```bash
grep -rn "NewVault()\|NewCredentialStore" --include=*.go .   # tests only
grep -n "credStore :=" internal/app/app.go                   # NewKeychain()
```

Observed: the vault has no non-test constructor call.
Expected: either the vault is wired and the keychain is a backend behind it, or
the vault is gone and the keychain is the documented answer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The ADR nocx-25k9 requires is written and merged, and it answers explicitly
  which store the shipped binary uses and why — keychain, vault, or vault with
  the keychain holding the master key.
- The composition root matches that ADR. If the vault is the answer, `app.go`
  constructs it and `NewCredentialStore` is on a live path; if the keychain is
  the answer, the vault and its tests are deleted rather than left to look
  load-bearing.
- The stale `CredentialStore` alias and its "only to avoid editing app.go in
  this wave" comment are resolved either way.
- No package in the repo exports an encryption path reachable only from its own
  tests.

title: ADR: is the UI kit hand-rolled or built on a headless library?
description:
The kit epic must not start with someone writing a button. Decide first.

Options to weigh, at minimum:
- Hand-rolled vanilla-TS components. No dependency, full control, matches the current frontend which uses no framework. Cost: we write and maintain accessibility (focus management, ARIA, keyboard operation of a custom select) ourselves, and that is the part hand-rolled kits get wrong.
- A headless component library (accessibility and keyboard behaviour provided, styling ours). Cost: a dependency, and most of them assume a framework — check that a genuinely framework-free one exists before treating this as available.
- Style the native controls only, no component layer. Cheapest. Cost: a native <select> cannot be styled to match on macOS, which is the exact complaint that opened this epic.

Constraint from the epic: this must NOT smuggle in a UI framework. If the only viable headless library needs React, that is an argument against the library, not an argument for React.

Also produce here: the component inventory (button, text input, search input, checkbox/toggle, select, list/nav rail, section heading, badge, empty state) and where each already exists in style.css so the migration reuses rather than rewrites.
acceptance_criteria: An ADR in docs/decisions/ records the choice, the alternatives weighed, and the component inventory the kit must cover; it is merged before any component is written.
notes: Superseded in framing by .internal/specs/2026-07-27-ui-shell-kit-and-theming-design.md section 4. The ADR's answer is: local nocx kit, Kobalte only behind wrappers, surfaces never import it directly; solid-ui/shadcn-for-Solid rejected. BUT the ADR must not be written until the spike in section 4.1 reports the pinned @kobalte/core version, its maintenance status and peer range against solid-js 1.9.14, the MEASURED gzip delta for the six primitives against the real production build, and the portal/Wails behaviour in section 4.2. If the spike fails, the fallback is local controls plus narrow a11y utilities.
close_reason: ADR-0014 records the platform-first per-primitive decision with the consumer evidence and the grep commands behind it. Declines a library on consumers rather than on cost, since the corrected measurement showed Kobalte DPT would have fitted the budget. Negative consequences recorded including the unstylable native select popup, the 300-500 line overlay core, the unverifiable Wails drag interaction, and the untested xterm focus-return path.

title: ADR: pick the frontend state store and map slice ownership
description:
The owner asked for zustand by name. Zustand does work outside React (vanilla store + subscribe), so it is a real candidate — but so is a ~50-line hand-rolled observable, and this frontend has no framework and few consumers. Decide with an argument, not by reflex.

Must be settled in the ADR:
- The store. Zustand vanilla vs hand-rolled observable vs an alternative. Weigh bundle size, devtools, and whether the team gains anything from a dependency at this consumer count.
- The state shape and slice ownership: tabs (list, active, per-tab title/cwd/status), placement, sidebar (active view, collapsed), settings revision.
- Reconciliation with AD-7: session id is server-authoritative. The store MIRRORS it and must never mint one. Say explicitly how a server-side change reaches the store.
- Reconciliation with AD-6: terminal render state stays in xterm.js and does NOT enter the store. Draw the line.
- What happens to SettingsObserver — does it write into the store, or is it replaced by it?
- Migration order, so the bugs already filed (nocx-98z6, nocx-nb8v, nocx-4ff.28, nocx-4ff.29) are not re-broken by the migration.
acceptance_criteria: An ADR in docs/decisions/ records the store choice, the state shape, which module owns each slice, and how it reconciles with AD-6 and AD-7; it is merged before any module is migrated.

title: Migrate Settings, Connections and the sidebar onto the kit — no raw native controls
description:
Every control on the Settings screen is a raw platform widget dropped into a
dark custom-styled app: a default macOS `<select>` with the system chrome and
scroll-wheel arrows for Tab placement, and unstyled `<input type=checkbox>` for
the toggles. Against the app's own dark surface they read as someone else's UI.

This is the migration half of the epic — it depends on the kit existing, so it
must not start before the kit ADR lands and the components are written.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No raw unstyled `<select>` or `<input type=checkbox>` remains in Settings,
  Connections, or the sidebar — each is a kit component.
- Controls match the app theme, including focus rings, hover, disabled and
  invalid states.
- Keyboard operation and screen-reader labels are preserved or improved
  relative to the native controls being replaced — a styled control that cannot
  be operated from the keyboard is a regression, not a fix.
- The "Default" / "Customized" / "Reset" affordance beside each row is part of
  the kit, rendered identically for every control type.
close_reason: Superseded and satisfied: Settings, Connections and the sidebar all render through the kit with zero raw native controls, enforced by nocx/no-raw-controls with an empty baseline rather than by review.

title: Cold start shows an empty CONNECTIONS panel — the sidebar opens on a tab-action view
description:
On a cold start the app shows an empty sidebar panel headed "CONNECTIONS" — a
wide grey column with a title and nothing in it, occupying a third of the
window. It reads as broken, and it is the first thing the user sees.

Cause, read on main 2026-07-26: `SidebarImpl` takes `views[0].id` as the initial
`activeViewId` (frontend/src/sidebar.ts:52) regardless of that view's action, and
the first registered view is Connections, whose action is `'tab'`
(frontend/src/main.ts:185-207). A `'tab'` view has no `mount` and therefore no
content container — so the panel opens on a view that can never fill it, and
shows only its title.

Two things to decide, not one:
- The immediate fix: the initial active view must be one that can actually
  render a panel, or the panel must start collapsed when no panel-view is
  selected.
- The design question behind it: the panel starts EXPANDED by default
  (collapsed only if localStorage says otherwise). For a terminal, an empty
  expanded panel on first run is the wrong default — starting collapsed is
  likely right. Confirm with the owner before changing the default.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Launch the app with no prior sidebar state (fresh profile / cleared
   localStorage key `nocx.sidebar.collapsed`).

Observed: a wide empty panel labelled CONNECTIONS beside the activity bar.
Expected: no dead empty panel — either a collapsed panel, or a panel showing a
view with real content.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A fresh launch never shows an expanded panel with no content in it.
- Selecting a `'tab'`-action view (Connections, Settings) opens its tab and does
  not leave the panel showing that view's empty header.
- A test asserts the initial state for a fresh profile.

title: Clicking a section in the Settings rail changes nothing in the content pane
description:
Clicking a section in the Settings rail does nothing visible. The rail
highlights the clicked item (Clipboard -> Interface) but the content pane on the
right is unchanged — both sections stay rendered in full, and the pane does not
scroll to the clicked one.

`scrollToSection` is wired to the nav buttons (frontend/src/settings-content.ts
~L250), so either the scroll target resolves to the wrong element, or the
content pane is not the scroll container, or with only two short sections there
is nothing to scroll and the interaction has no effect by construction.

That last possibility matters for the fix: if the rail is a scroll-spy, it is
inherently useless at this content size, and the honest fix may be to make the
rail FILTER to the selected section rather than scroll to it. Decide which
before implementing.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings.
2. Click "Clipboard" in the rail, then click "Interface".

Observed 2026-07-26: only the rail's own highlight moves. The right pane shows
CLIPBOARD and INTERFACE both, unchanged, at the same scroll position.

Expected: selecting a section visibly changes what the right pane shows.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Clicking a rail section produces a visible change in the content pane every
  time, including when all sections already fit on screen.
- The rail's active highlight always agrees with what the pane is showing.
- A test asserts the pane's visible content after a section click, not just the
  rail's class list.
close_reason: Fixed as an acceptance criterion of the settings migration (nocx-eerg). Selecting a section in the rail now always produces a visible change in the content pane, pinned by a test named for this bead.

title: Settings renders its chrome twice — two search boxes, two modified toggles
description:
The Settings tab renders its chrome twice: two "Search settings…" inputs and two
"Modified" toggles, side by side in two panes.

Cause, read on main 2026-07-26: `SettingsContent` builds a rail with its own
search input and Modified toggle (frontend/src/settings-content.ts:60-82), while
`SettingsView` independently builds a second search input and a
"Modified only (N)" checkbox in the content pane (frontend/src/settings.ts:
315-344). The rail was added around a view that already had this chrome, and the
old one was never removed.

Decide which one survives — do not keep both wired to one state. The rail's
version is the one that fits the two-pane layout; the view's belongs to a
single-pane design that no longer exists.

This is the cheap, visible half of nocx-vxqj (the UI-kit epic) and is fixable
now without waiting for it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings (Cmd+, or the gear in the activity bar).

Observed: two search boxes and two modified-filter checkboxes are visible at
once — one pair in the middle rail, one pair in the right content pane.

Expected: one search input and one modified filter for the screen.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Exactly one search input and one modified-filter control exist in the Settings
  DOM.
- Search still filters rows and hides sections that end up empty.
- The modified filter still works and still shows the modified count.
- The dead chrome is deleted, not hidden with CSS.
close_reason: Fixed as an acceptance criterion of the settings migration (nocx-eerg), not as a separate patch — which was the plan recorded in the epic: fixing it before the rewrite would have been throwaway work, and 'preserve current behaviour' taken literally would have reproduced it. The migrated surface has exactly one search box and one modified filter, both in the rail, and both are pinned by tests named for this bead.

title: Switching tabs drops keystrokes until the user clicks into the editor
description:
After switching tabs, the first keystrokes are dropped — the user has to click
inside the editor before typing registers. Every tab switch costs a click.

Suspected area: focus is not moved to the newly-activated tab's input target on
activation (ADR-0004 InputTarget registry). Related to, but distinct from, the
bug where creating a new tab breaks input in the first tab: this one affects a
tab that is otherwise healthy and is fixed by a click; that one is not.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open two tabs.
2. Click the other tab in the tab strip to switch to it.
3. Immediately start typing, without clicking in the terminal area.

Observed: nothing is typed. After clicking once inside the editor, typing works.
Expected: the activated tab's input has focus, so typing goes straight in.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Switching tabs by click, by keyboard shortcut, and by closing a tab (focus
  falls to a neighbour) all leave the newly-active tab's input focused.
- Typing immediately after a switch registers the first character — none are
  dropped.
- Focus lands on the correct target for the tab's surface type: the editor for a
  terminal tab, and NOT stolen from a text field the user is using in a Settings
  or Connections tab.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
CONCRETE REPRODUCTION from CI, in case it helps: [chromium] e2e/click-focus.spec.ts:26 fails on macos-latest at line 41, which is the PRECONDITION rather than the assertion under test — after an explicit document.activeElement.blur(), focus returns to .nocx-editor-input within the 5s poll. Under webkit the same test passes.

Isolated evidence: this was one of 11 e2e failures on main; the other 10 were all one unrelated defect (bracketed paste, nocx-hi2) and are fixed on branch shady2k/nocx-hi2-bracketed-paste-gate, leaving this one alone in CI run 30217202549. So it is now reproducible without any other failure masking it. The test's comment at lines 43-50 already describes the suspected mechanism: the bounce handler bails when focus is already inside the xterm container.

title: [epic] Authoritative frontend state: one store, not per-module fields
description:
Observed 2026-07-26 on main: switching tab placement to Vertical leaves the tab list empty, and switching back to Horizontal does not restore it — the strip is swapped in place at the composition root (main.ts L157-L178, tm.replaceStrip) while tab state lives inside TabManager, so the two disagree. Related symptom: creating a second tab leaves the first tab unable to accept input, and switching tabs needs a click into the editor first — input ownership is another piece of state reduced in more than one place. nocx-aok already records the same shape for prompt-cycle state.

The owner asked: where is our centralised state, zustand? Today there is none. State is spread across TabManager fields, SidebarImpl fields, module-level closures in main.ts and the Go settings registry, and the modules resynchronise by calling each other.

SCOPE: pick the store (zustand works outside React, but a hand-rolled observable is also on the table — this is an ADR, not a foregone conclusion); define the frontend state shape and who owns each slice against AD-6 and AD-7 (server-authoritative session id must stay authoritative — the store mirrors it, never invents it); migrate tabs, placement, sidebar and settings-revision onto it; delete the per-module copies.

EXPLICITLY OUT: adopting a UI framework (React/Svelte/Vue). A state store is not a rendering framework and this epic must not smuggle one in. Terminal render state stays in xterm.js per AD-6 and does NOT move into the store.

DECISION NEEDED FIRST (ADR): store choice and the slice ownership map. The individual placement/input bugs filed alongside this epic may be fixed before it lands — they are the evidence for it, not blocked by it.
acceptance_criteria: Tab list, active tab, tab placement, sidebar view/collapse and settings revision live in one observable store that every UI module reads from and writes through; no app module keeps a private copy of that state; changing placement, active tab or sidebar view updates every dependent surface without a manual re-render call; a test asserts a single state change propagates to two independent consumers.
notes:
2026-07-26: this epic's 'EXPLICITLY OUT: adopting a UI framework' constraint was written believing a framework decision already existed to respect. It does not — see nocx-6zu5. The vanilla-TS setup came from the M0 scaffold commit and was never chosen against alternatives. The store choice here (zustand vs hand-rolled vs signals) is partly determined by that answer, so nocx-ycet.1 now depends on nocx-6zu5. If the UI-layer ADR lands on reactive primitives, this epic's ADR may be subsumed by it rather than run separately.
ZUSTAND: NO. Asked directly by the owner 2026-07-26; coordinator and codex agree independently.

If the UI-layer ADR (nocx-6zu5) lands on Svelte 5, the framework brings its own fine-grained reactive state. Adding Zustand means a second subscription system, a second model for derived state and batching, adapters between the two, and a standing ambiguity about whether a slice belongs in framework state or the store. That is more opportunities for parallel sources of truth — the exact failure this epic exists to end. Zustand's vanilla core does work outside React, but its main draw is escaping React's own state model, which is not a problem we would have.

THE GO-AUTHORITY QUESTION DOES NOT CHANGE THIS. Session IDs are server-authoritative (AD-7) and settings arrive with a revision from the Go registry, but that calls for explicit authority and transition rules, not a framework-independent reactive container. The shape:

  Go authority
      -> typed responses/events
  framework-neutral clients and transition functions (plain .ts)
      -> accepted state transitions only
  framework application state (small reactive module)
      -> components

Wire parsing, revision validation, session transition rules and command construction stay in ordinary TypeScript. Encode authority in the type: a session state union where no transition can produce serverSessionId except by handling the backend's successful open response, and a settings snapshot carrying its revision, where an incoming snapshot must pass the revision policy before replacing the local mirror.

DO NOT abstract the reactive layer so the framework can supposedly be swapped later. A framework replacement rewrites the component layer and its bindings regardless; keeping protocol and domain logic plain is the valuable half, and the rest is speculative architecture.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS EPIC: nocx-ycet.1 was scoped as 'pick the store'. That question is largely answered by nocx-6zu5 and this note. Re-scope it to defining the slice ownership map and the authority/transition boundary above, rather than choosing a library.

title: [epic] UI kit: one component vocabulary, reused instead of re-created
description:
Observed 2026-07-26 on main: the Settings screen renders two search inputs and two 'Modified' toggles side by side (settings.ts builds its own chrome at L315-L344, settings-content.ts builds a second rail at L60-L82), and the controls are raw platform widgets — a default macOS <select> and unstyled checkboxes — inside an otherwise dark, custom-styled app. It looks unfinished because each surface grew its own controls.

The rule the owner stated: we do NOT create a new component for every need. There is one UI kit, and before writing a control you reuse what exists.

SCOPE: extract the component vocabulary that already exists in style.css and the ad-hoc renderers into an explicit kit (button, text input, search input, checkbox/toggle, select, list/nav rail, section heading, badge, empty state); restyle the native controls so they match the app theme in both light and dark; migrate Settings, Connections and the sidebar onto it; delete the duplicated chrome; and add the guard that keeps the next surface from re-hand-rolling.

EXPLICITLY OUT: a design-system package published outside this repo; theming/customisation beyond what nocx-8yg already owns; any framework migration — that decision belongs to the frontend-state epic, and this epic must not pre-empt it.

DECISION NEEDED FIRST (ADR): whether the kit is hand-rolled vanilla-TS components or adopts an existing headless library. Do not start implementation before that ADR lands.
acceptance_criteria: Every control the user touches in Settings, Connections and the sidebar is rendered by a component from a single documented kit (frontend/src/ui/), with no raw unstyled native <select>/<input type=checkbox> left in an app surface; a written inventory lists each kit component and the surfaces using it; a lint or test fails when an app module hand-rolls a control the kit already provides.
notes: 2026-07-26: the ADR here asks hand-rolled components vs a headless library, and notes most headless libraries assume a framework. That is unanswerable while nocx-6zu5 is open, so nocx-vxqj.2 now depends on it.
close_reason: Every control the user touches comes from frontend/src/ui/, the inventory is written at ui/README.md, and three lint rules fail the build when a surface hand-rolls what the kit owns — raw controls, inline markup duplicating a component class, and colour literals. All three baselines are EMPTY, which was the epic's own closing condition. Every kit export has a production consumer, verified by grep: the four that did not (PageBody, PageRail, Field, EmptyState) were either composed by Page or adopted by the surface they were written for.

title: [epic] The test suite is green and stays green
description:
Carved out of nocx-k0xk, which was an area and not a deliverable — it held 17 children spanning e2e rot, CI configuration, linting and mutation testing, and could never close.

One deliverable: the suite tells the truth about the product. Today it does not — 13 e2e tests failed in all three CI runs that were diffed, and the enabler is that Playwright is not in the per-commit gate, so dead selectors rot unobserved between PRs.

Children, in dependency order: nocx-qkp (6 of 9 specs cannot authenticate on the headless path, which blocks reproducing anything locally), nocx-bw2 (triage the remaining failures), then nocx-9ci, nocx-heq, nocx-epm (the specific fixes), plus nocx-zaj (Go tests flake under load — and a data race in internal/ssh, which is production code, not a slow test).

DONE WHEN: the full suite passes repeatedly under parallel load on both projects, the Go race detector is clean, and a red suite is observable before a PR rather than after.
acceptance_criteria: the full suite passes repeatedly under parallel load on both projects, the Go race detector is clean, and a red suite is observable before a PR rather than after.
close_reason:
Epic complete: 6/6. The suite is green and the flakes are gone by construction rather than by tolerance.

nocx-bw2 — from 13 failures to 0. The last one was a product bug (setActive never repainted), not a stale test.
nocx-qkp — 9 of 10 specs on the token-aware harness; seed.spec.ts stays off it deliberately, having no session to authenticate.
nocx-9ci — the spec stopped clicking a button that alt-screen hides by design.
nocx-zaj — Go waits made event-driven, verified with -race -count=5 over both packages.
nocx-epm, nocx-heq — e2e duration-waits replaced with condition-waits.

The measurable outcome: the suite runs in 18.1s against 57.5s before, because it no longer spends its wall clock outliving worst-case sleeps. That number is the evidence the fixes are real rather than retimed.

NOT done, and deliberately out: Playwright is still not in the per-commit gate. That is nocx-63l and it is gated on the suite being RELIABLY green, which two green days do not prove.

Carry-forward recorded separately: WPEWebProcess crashes on teardown (heap corruption in exit handlers, no symbols, upstream). Chromium never does. So a 'browser closed unexpectedly' in webkit logs is not automatically a test defect, and if nocx-heq's rotation returns, that is the first place to look.

title: [epic] Credential correctness: stored secrets are actually used and correctly derived
description:
Carved out of nocx-6ek, which was an area and not a deliverable — every new persistence bug landed in it, so it could never close.

Two defects on the credential path, both on the same code and both cheap to verify:
